summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for Yozgat province. That absence records the absence of documented divergence from the national position, not local safety: the rules set out below reach Yozgat unchanged.

Yozgat stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward LGBTI+ people has hardened into formal state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family", records instructions issued to public institutions under that banner and, for the first time in years, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation; expression and artistic freedom were restricted and events cancelled or banned.

The same review counts 313 liberty violations in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year, alongside 299 detention decisions; 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year; 61 travel bans; and private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, among them obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy. Six right-to-life violations were recorded, three of them hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the most affected group.

A leaked omnibus draft, the "11th Judicial Package", was reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years' imprisonment, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years' imprisonment, patients up to three, with pretrial detention possible.

Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. Human Rights Watch warns that it would drive treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

Document checks are a standing exposure for a trans visitor anywhere in Turkey. Foreign nationals must produce original photo identification at transit checkpoints, and police stops for background checks were used against trans women in Istanbul in 2025. Every such interaction is an occasion on which a passport gender marker is compared against presentation, and fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira are attached to non-compliance with the identification rule.

Lethal violence and asymmetric state response are documented nationally. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; rights groups demanded an independent investigation, and opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025. Prison Insider's country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusal of hospital transfer, and administration operating on a binary basis with no staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, risking the profiling of trans patients in official records.
tangentialFactors:
Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

Street-level enforcement in Istanbul indicates how the national regime operates in practice. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that enforcement was already being applied although the new law had not yet been passed.

The pending legislative package has functioned as if enacted before enactment. As of October 2025 the Erdoğan government framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people, and the draft had not been passed when reported.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the depth of the regime rather than as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
For Turkish residents, the 2025 figures are cumulative: 313 liberty violations, 299 detention decisions, 89 torture or ill-treatment cases against 51 the previous year, private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, 61 travel bans, and the first closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation in years under "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions.

Obstruction of hormone therapy is recorded within the private-life category, so continuity of transition-related care is itself a documented point of interference, not merely a background condition of residency.

Placement of trans prisoners follows registered sex: a trans man was held in a women's prison, and custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers in the Poyraz case reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Turkish rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation.

The September 2025 Health Ministry regulation, which followed the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular adding "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, bars hospitals from recording the "other" option and requires e-reports to be issued. Its effect on residents is the creation of a formal record category that can be read in subsequent official interactions.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. Transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence, and refusals of hospital transfer occur out of fear of other male prisoners.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory concerns Yozgat province directly: there is no record of local police practice, local prosecutions, local Pride or nightlife activity, or local health facilities providing transition-related care in Yozgat. Whether the national pattern plays out in the province at the same intensity is unresolved.

The status of the 11th Judicial Package is unresolved as of the latest source. Human Rights Watch reported it as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025 and it had not been passed when reported; no later source in this inventory confirms whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn, and no source establishes whether enforcement has continued in advance of enactment.

The reported provisions of the draft are drawn from a leaked text as described by Human Rights Watch rather than from a published statute, so the final wording of any enacted measure is not sourced here.

The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 is described through reporting and a provincial circular; the text of the ministry regulation itself is not available in this inventory, and its precise scope for private hospitals is unresolved.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is retained only as historical evidence of the regime's depth, not as a statement of current law.

The counts in the Kaos GL 2025 review are national tallies with no provincial breakdown, so they cannot be attributed to Yozgat.
